blocks.text: At 20:00 a day team tells the night doctor, 'Bed 7 is fine, just needs bloods.' Nobody mentions that the bloods are a repeat potassium after treatment for a dangerously high result, or that the result must be acted on within the hour. At 06:00 it is still unchecked. The patient was never ignored; the information simply did not travel.

blocks.markdown: Hospital care is delivered by **teams over time**. Every shift change, ward move and weekend is a point where information can be lost. **Handover** is the transfer of information and responsibility for patients from one clinician or team to another, and **documentation** is the durable record that lets anyone, at any time, understand what happened and why. Both are core clinical skills, not administrative chores, and as a student you will already be asked to contribute to both.

blocks.title: Clinical handover
blocks.text: **Handover** is the transfer of professional responsibility and accountability for some or all aspects of care for a patient, or group of patients, to another person or professional group, on a temporary or permanent basis. Good handover is accurate, concise, structured and has a clear recipient who accepts it.

blocks.markdown:
### A structure for handover

A structure makes sure the essentials are never left to memory. **SBAR** (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is widely used in UK health services, and some use the extended **ISBAR** with an Identify step at the front. Whatever the template, a safe handover contains the following.

blocks.caption: SBAR applied to a handover
rows: Who you are, patient name and identifiers, location, and the main problem now
'This is Mrs A, bed 4, admitted today with cellulitis of the left leg.'
Relevant history, reason for admission, key treatments, allergies and baseline
'She has type 2 diabetes and is allergic to penicillin; on IV antibiotics since 14:00.'
Current condition, latest observations, trend and your concern
'Temperature settling, early warning score fell from 4 to 2 over the day.'
Outstanding tasks with times, what to watch for, and the escalation plan
'Repeat blood tests at 22:00; if the score reaches 5 or more, review urgently.'

blocks.markdown:
Two parts of handover are most often missed and deserve special attention.

**Outstanding tasks** should be specific: *what* must be done, *by when*, and *who* is responsible. 'Needs bloods' is not a task; 'repeat potassium at 22:00, act on result, treat if above the local threshold' is. **Escalation plans** set out what to do if the patient deteriorates: the observation or score that triggers a review, who to call, and the patient's agreed ceiling of treatment, including resuscitation status, where one has been recorded.

blocks.title: Turning a vague handover into a structured one
blocks.prompt: At the end of the afternoon, a student hears this handover: 'Mr Okoro in bay 3, the hernia lad, is doing OK. Might need something for pain. Check him later.' In fact he is a 66-year-old man, 1 day after an elective inguinal hernia repair, passing urine but with a urine output the nurse is watching. He has a documented allergy to codeine. His night-time analgesia is not yet written up. Restructure the handover.

steps.text: Situation: identify the patient fully (name and date of birth or hospital number, bay and bed) and state the problem: 1 day after elective inguinal hernia repair, pain control and urine output to be monitored.
Background: relevant history and the safety-critical facts, namely the recorded codeine allergy and the fact that regular analgesia has not been prescribed for the night.
Assessment: report the latest observations and the trend, and the nursing concern about urine output with a time of the last measurement.
Recommendation with tasks: prescribe night analgesia that avoids codeine, check urine output at a stated time, and ask the nurse to inform the doctor if there is no urine for a specified period.
Escalation: name the trigger (for example a rising early warning score or no urine output by the agreed time), who is covering and how to contact them.

blocks.answer: A structured handover names the patient and problem, flags the codeine allergy, states the outstanding prescription and urine output task with times, and gives clear escalation triggers and a contact.

blocks.title: Closed-loop communication
blocks.text: Safe handover is two-way. The recipient repeats back key information and tasks, asks questions and confirms who now owns each task. Handing over in a quiet place, away from interruptions, and using a written or electronic list reduces loss of detail.

blocks.markdown:
### Writing in the clinical notes

The notes are a legal and clinical record. UK professional guidance (the General Medical Council's standards for good medical practice and the Nursing and Midwifery Council's equivalent) expects records to be clear, accurate, legible and contemporaneous (written at the time or as soon as possible afterwards). Every entry should be:

- **dated and timed** (24-hour clock),
- **signed**, with the author's printed name, role and professional registration number where applicable (students follow local rules and usually add their student status and have entries countersigned by a registered clinician),
- **legible**, in black ink where handwritten, or typed in the electronic record,
- **factual and objective**, distinguishing what was observed or measured from opinion,
- free of **unapproved abbreviations** and of offensive or speculative remarks,
- corrected by a **single line through the error**, with the correction dated and signed, never by erasure or correction fluid.

blocks.title: Writing a good note entry
blocks.prompt: At 14:25 on 12 March you reviewed a 74-year-old woman, Mrs Brown, who had a fall on the ward. She was found sitting on the floor, said she slipped on her way to the toilet, and had no head strike. Her pulse is 82 per minute, blood pressure 138 over 76 mmHg and she has a 3 cm bruise on the left forearm. Your registrar examined her and asked for a medication review. Write the structure of an acceptable entry.

steps.text: Start with the header: date 12/03, time 14:25, location and the patient's identifiers (name, date of birth or hospital number).
Record the event factually: found sitting on the floor by the bed at about 14:15, reported slipping on the way to the toilet, no head strike, no loss of consciousness reported by the patient.
Record the findings: pulse 82 per minute, blood pressure 138/76 mmHg, 3 cm bruise on the left forearm, no other injury found. Use measured values rather than adjectives.
Record the plan and who made decisions: examined with the registrar; medication review requested; falls precautions in place; plan to repeat observations per ward policy.
End with a signature: printed name, role (medical student), the time, and ask a registered clinician to countersign according to local policy.

blocks.answer: A good entry is dated, timed, factual, includes measured findings, a clear plan and who made it, and is signed with name and role.

blocks.markdown:
### How poor handover causes harm

Poor handover contributes to patient harm through **omission** (tasks never done, results never reviewed), **distortion** (wrong patient, wrong dose, wrong urgency), **ambiguity** (unclear who is responsible), and **loss of context** (a deterioration trend that nobody tells the next shift about). Typical consequences include delayed treatment, repeated investigations, missed allergies, medication errors and unplanned readmission. Contributory conditions are well known: interruptions, noise, fatigue, unstructured conversations, information carried only in memory and ambiguity about who has accepted responsibility. These are **system factors**, which is why the answer is structure, standard templates and protected time rather than blame.

blocks.caption: Weak and strong practice
rows: SBAR or ISBAR with a written list
Trigger, contact and ceiling of treatment stated
Listener repeats back and accepts responsibility
Dated, timed, signed and legible entry

blocks.title: Never amend records after the event to hide an error
blocks.text: If an entry is wrong, strike it through with one line, add the correction and date and sign it. Altering or backdating records can be treated as dishonesty and is a serious professional matter.

points: A structured handover such as SBAR includes patient identity, key background and allergies, current status and trend, specific outstanding tasks with times and owners, and an escalation plan.
Good clinical notes are contemporaneous, dated, timed, signed, legible, factual and corrected only by a single line with a signed correction.
Poor handover harms patients through omitted tasks, distorted information and unclear responsibility, and the main protections are structure, protected time and closed-loop communication.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT part of a handover using SBAR?

options.text: Situation
Background
Assessment
Blame

distractorRationale.a: Situation is the first element and states the current problem.
distractorRationale.b: Background gives the history, allergies and treatment so far.
distractorRationale.c: Assessment gives the current condition and trend.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: SBAR stands for Situation, Background, Assessment and Recommendation; blame has no role.

questions.explanation: SBAR stands for Situation, Background, Assessment and Recommendation. The structure aims to make sure every handover includes the same essential elements.

questions.stem: At the end of a night shift, a doctor hands over a patient on a continuous infusion with 'keep an eye on him'. Which change would make the handover most useful to the day team?

options.text: State the specific task, such as 'check the glucose at 08:00 and adjust per the protocol', and the trigger for escalation and whom to call
Hand over verbally in the corridor so that it is faster
Leave out the background to keep it short
Tell the day team to ask the patient what needs doing

questions.correctOptionText: State the specific task, such as 'check the glucose at 08:00 and adjust per the protocol', and the trigger for escalation and whom to call

distractorRationale.a: Correct: specific tasks with times and escalation triggers remove ambiguity.
distractorRationale.b: Corridor handovers are interrupted and increase loss of information.
distractorRationale.c: Omitting background removes the context needed to interpret change.
distractorRationale.d: Patients cannot be relied on to supply the clinical plan.

questions.explanation: Vague instructions such as 'keep an eye on him' leave unclear what is to be done, when, and what to do if it goes wrong. Specific tasks, timings and escalation triggers allow the next team to act safely.

questions.stem: A newly qualified doctor writes in the notes, in pencil, 'Pt much better, plan as before' with no date, time or signature. Which problem is most serious from a record-keeping standpoint?

options.text: The entry is not dated, timed or signed, so nobody can tell who wrote it or when, and it is vague and impermanent
The entry is too short to be useful, but that is its only problem
It is acceptable because the author knew what it meant
The only issue is that the handwriting may be untidy

questions.correctOptionText: The entry is not dated, timed or signed, so nobody can tell who wrote it or when, and it is vague and impermanent

distractorRationale.a: Correct: dating, timing, signature and permanence are essential, and 'much better' is not objective.
distractorRationale.b: Brevity is not the only fault; the entry also lacks identifiers and a signature.
distractorRationale.c: Records must be understood by others, not just the author.
distractorRationale.d: Legibility is one issue but not the main one here.

questions.explanation: Entries must be dated, timed, signed, written in permanent form and factual, so that any reader can tell who documented what and when. 'Much better' and 'plan as before' give no measurable information.

questions.stem: You notice you wrote the wrong date in an entry earlier in the day. What is the correct way to correct it?

options.text: Strike through the error with a single line, write the correct entry, and date and sign the correction
Cover the error with correction fluid
Tear out the page and rewrite it
Scribble over it until it is unreadable

questions.correctOptionText: Strike through the error with a single line, write the correct entry, and date and sign the correction

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the original remains readable and the correction is attributable.
distractorRationale.b: Correction fluid hides the original and can suggest concealment.
distractorRationale.c: Removing pages destroys part of the legal record.
distractorRationale.d: Obliterating text prevents anyone reading the original entry.

questions.explanation: A single line leaves the original legible, and a dated and signed correction shows who changed it and when. Concealing or destroying records can be seen as dishonest.

questions.stem: A patient is transferred from the emergency department to a ward. The ward team do not learn that the patient is on warfarin, and a procedure the next morning is not delayed for the required checks. Which feature of poor handover does this best illustrate?

options.text: Omission of safety-critical information, which allowed a preventable risk to reach the patient
Excessive detail in the handover
The patient's own fault for not mentioning it
An unavoidable event that no system could prevent

questions.correctOptionText: Omission of safety-critical information, which allowed a preventable risk to reach the patient

distractorRationale.a: Correct: missing high-risk information (anticoagulation) is a classic way handover causes harm.
distractorRationale.b: The problem here is missing, not excessive, information.
distractorRationale.c: Safety depends on clinicians passing on information, not relying on patients to do so.
distractorRationale.d: Structured handover and medicines reconciliation exist to prevent exactly this.

questions.explanation: Omission of safety-critical information, such as anticoagulation, allergies or recent changes in condition, is one of the commonest ways poor handover causes harm. Structured templates that prompt for medications and risks reduce this.

questions.stem: During a Friday evening handover to the weekend team, a doctor says a patient 'has a result pending'. Which additional information most improves safety?

options.text: Which test, who will look for the result, by when, and what action to take if it is abnormal
A comment that the result is probably normal
The name of the laboratory technician
A request that the weekend team ignore the result unless asked

questions.correctOptionText: Which test, who will look for the result, by when, and what action to take if it is abnormal

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it assigns ownership, timing and action, preventing the result being lost.
distractorRationale.b: Predicting the result does not ensure it is reviewed.
distractorRationale.c: Laboratory staff names do not help follow-up.
distractorRationale.d: Ignoring results is itself a risk.

questions.explanation: A pending result is a classic outstanding task that is lost at transitions of care unless ownership, timing and action are explicit. Naming who will check, when, and what to do converts a vague risk into a controlled task.

questions.stem: True or false: as a medical student, you may make a clinical entry in the notes without any signature, provided you write your own name in your own diary.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Entries in the notes must be dated, timed and signed within the record itself, with your name and role, and students usually need a registered clinician to countersign. A private diary entry does not make the record attributable.

questions.stem: A patient with sepsis is stable at the end of your shift but needs repeat lactate and cultures reviewed at 01:00, and is not for admission to intensive care according to a documented decision. Describe the structure and key content of a safe handover for this patient.
markingGuide: Uses a recognised structure such as SBAR or ISBAR and states identity of patient and location
Situation and background: sepsis, source if known, treatment started and allergies
Assessment: latest observations, early warning score and trend
Outstanding tasks with times and owners: lactate and cultures review at 01:00, who will do it and the action if abnormal
Escalation plan: trigger such as rising early warning score, who to call, and the documented treatment ceiling (not for intensive care)
Closed loop: recipient repeats back and accepts responsibility; delivered in a quiet setting
questions.explanation: A safe handover pairs a clear structure with specific tasks, owners, timings and an escalation plan, including any agreed limits on treatment. Confirming that the receiver has understood the plan closes the loop.

questions.stem: List the features of a good entry in the clinical notes and explain why each one matters to patient safety or accountability.
markingGuide: Dated and timed, so the sequence of care can be reconstructed
Signed with printed name and role (and registration number if applicable), so the author is identifiable
Legible, permanent or typed, so others can read it
Factual and objective, separating observations from opinion
Avoids unapproved abbreviations and offensive or speculative language
Errors corrected by a single line with signed correction so the original remains readable
questions.explanation: Each feature either lets the next clinician understand what happened or lets the record stand up to scrutiny. Together they make the notes a reliable and legally defensible record of care.

questions.stem: Explain how poor handover contributes to patient harm, giving at least three mechanisms and suggesting a system-level measure that reduces each.
markingGuide: Omission of information or tasks, for example results not reviewed; countermeasure: structured template and task list with owners and times
Distortion or ambiguity, for example wrong patient or unclear urgency; countermeasure: use of two identifiers and standard language such as SBAR
Loss of context or trend information; countermeasure: include latest observations and trend in the handover and electronic summary
Interruptions or poor setting; countermeasure: protected time and quiet space
No acceptance of responsibility; countermeasure: closed-loop communication with read-back
Recognises these are system factors and links to learning rather than blame
questions.explanation: Harm arises when information is missing, distorted or not owned, and each mechanism has a matching structural fix. Framing the fixes at system level reflects the patient safety principle that individuals work within systems.
